speakers: Jan van Eck (CEO, Van Eck, guest)
summary:
Jan van Eck (CEO of Van Eck, $230bn AUM) argues big outside forces (fiscal and monetary policy, deregulation, technology, demographics) shape markets and that long-term rate regimes bias history.
He stays fully invested in equities except in aggressive Fed tightening, prefers real assets to bonds as diversifier, rebalances, and uses valuation only as a secondary check inside trends.
Views: India and international diversification, AI/tech judged by market structure and moats, caution on narrative stocks without valuation support.

coverage.note: Intro, father's philosophy; macro forces shape markets, rejection of CAPM
Long trends: demographics, 40-year falling rates bias, company data feeding macro, host on one-regime data
Patterns: Fed down payments, country deregulation, India, fiscal deficits, monetary stance, non-bank lending
Fed tightening and equities; technology pattern recognition, railroad analogy, Nvidia, markets missing forces
Psychology of forecasting, bond market disconnects, currency pegs, stay invested, 60/40 and real assets
Rebalancing, liquidity shocks, diversification and hidden exposures, Bitcoin vs gold
Bitcoin cycle, emerging markets and India, valuation within trends, price-to-sales
Valuation limits, moats, nuclear and copper, narratives, sizing, alt-manager valuation round trip
Valuation as comfort, ETF policy, passive flows and dispersion, bond ETF liquidity
Retail behaviour, India underappreciated; closing and legal disclaimer

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: there are forces in the world government policy, government spending policy, fiscal policy, monetary policy, how much money is being printed, technology, war, these outside forces will shape financial markets
claims.claim: Outside forces (fiscal and monetary policy, money printing, technology, war) shape financial markets, so portfolios should be built from these forces rather than from market-internal relationships.
claims.indicator: fiscal policy, monetary policy, money printed, technology, war
claims.testable: partly: each force can be proxied by a series, but the set is broad

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: Financial theory over the last hundred uh and especially the last 50 years started to try to look at the markets as a science.
claims.claim: Academic finance (CAPM-style stock-to-market laws) treats markets as a self-contained system, which he rejects as a basis for building portfolios because markets sit inside a larger world.
claims.testable: no: a philosophical stance on method

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: some developments get priced into the markets over a longer period of time because some of these trends are are super long
claims.claim: Very long trends are priced into markets slowly, so a long time lens helps sort the daily information flow.
claims.testable: partly: needs a defined long-trend variable and a pricing lag test

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So some of these very long-term trends are are very powerful and you can't really escape them.
claims.claim: Demographics is the clearest long trend: China's population is certain to shrink sharply over a century and India has overtaken it as most populous, though the investment implication is separate from the trend itself.
claims.conditions: trend is certain, implications are not
claims.testable: yes: population projections are public, mapping to returns is hard

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: long-term interest rates in the United States have been falling over that entire time period from high double digits, right?
claims.claim: US long-term rates fell from the early 1980s to about 1% in COVID, a long tailwind for both bonds and stocks that he believes has ended, so the macro regime is now different.
claims.direction: falling rates: bonds and stocks up; regime now over
claims.testable: yes: regime split on long rates

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: whatever charts you're looking at over the last 40 years have this big bias to them of a falling interest rate and falling inflationary environment
claims.claim: Any 40-year chart or backtest carries a built-in bias from falling rates and falling inflation, so results must be read with that regime in mind.
claims.testable: yes: split sample by rate and inflation regime

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: that big macro insight about the political changes in China came from individual data points and conversations
claims.claim: Macro insights can start from company-level data points and conversations (e.g. firms trading with China in 1992), so bottom-up observation feeds macro views.
claims.testable: no: anecdotal sourcing of ideas

claims.speaker: Alex (host)
claims.quote: you can look at it from the other perspective of it's one data point, right?
claims.claim: Forty years of falling rates is effectively one regime observation; it let people lever up and refinance rather than repay, and if the environment shifts and persists the numbers studied for 40 years change completely.
claims.testable: partly: regime break tests have few independent observations

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the fact that they didn't require 10 or 20% down to buy a house
claims.claim: The Fed's biggest error before the crisis was allowing mortgages with almost no money down, which biased risk-taking because borrowers risked little of their own money.
claims.conditions: low-rate era with lax lending rules
claims.testable: no: historical judgment, not a signal

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: If a if a government central government in a country is creating a pro business environment with by deregulating by the rule of law that is a great a great signal that they're probably going to be increasing corporate profits
claims.claim: Country-level deregulation and rule of law signal rising corporate profits and therefore good stock returns ahead (China, then India).
claims.direction: long equities of the deregulating country
claims.conditions: works best with political consensus; many countries are mixed
claims.testable: partly: needs a coded deregulation index

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: when you have a green light like I think you have with India now then you take it right
claims.claim: India currently has a green light from deregulation, digitization and cell-phone access, with the highest GDP growth in the world this year, so he would take the opportunity.
claims.testable: no: single market view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: if they're running 6% of of uh GDP fiscal deficits, then they're, as I like to say, putting two feet on the gas pedal
claims.claim: A balanced budget is not stimulative while a deficit around 6% of GDP strongly stimulates the economy, so the fiscal deficit is a key thing to watch.
claims.testable: yes: fiscal deficit series is public

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: to take that out and just boil it down to what's our fiscal policy
claims.claim: Remove politicians' names and reduce the debate to fiscal policy to judge whether conditions are extreme or normal and keep emotion out of the analysis.
claims.testable: no: a framing discipline

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you can get a general sense of whether the Fed and Treasury are stimulating monetary policy or they're tightening it
claims.claim: Even though the same data points no longer work, one can still read whether the Fed and Treasury are stimulating or tightening, which defines the monetary regime.
claims.testable: yes: stance can be coded from policy rate changes

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: because lending has basically moved away from banks.
claims.claim: Because lending has moved from banks to non-bank lenders, monetary data series are not comparable with those of 40 years ago, so old relationships need care.
claims.testable: partly: shares can be measured but effect on signals untested

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: equity exposure, right? Whenever the Fed is slamming the brakes on.
claims.claim: When the Fed is hiking rapidly (2022: 1% to 4%) that is the time to worry about equity exposure.
claims.testable: yes: change in policy rate vs equity returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the likelihood was inflation was kind of in a in an area that didn't give the Fed a big budget to cut to cut short-term rates
claims.claim: Coming into this year he expected no monetary policy change because inflation left the Fed little room to cut short rates despite presidential pressure.
claims.indicator: inflation level vs Fed cut room
claims.testable: partly: a one-time view but the rule (inflation limits cuts) can be tested

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So much of market movement can be explained by by technology
claims.claim: Technology explains much of market movement but is the hardest pattern to turn into a signal.
claims.testable: no: no defined series

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: it is true that railroad stock prices peaked before the Transnational Railroad was built, but you have to take take another step and look at the market structure.
claims.claim: Railroad stocks peaking before the transcontinental line was finished does not make it a simple bubble, because a full network (market structure) was what created value; judge tech cycles by structure, not price run-up.
claims.conditions: networks and ecosystems where winners survive
claims.testable: partly: historical analogy hard to code

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you can't just take every disruptive technology and and just sort of call it a bubble
claims.claim: Disruptive technologies differ: electricity utilities and refineries saw capacity match demand with stable buildouts, so not every rally in a new technology is a bubble.
claims.indicator: capacity vs demand in technology buildout
claims.testable: partly: capacity versus demand data exist per industry

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: if I look at a company like Nvidia today, they've got a lot of the ecosystem.
claims.claim: Nvidia's ecosystem could give it an economic moat and survivor status in 10 years, though AI will still have booms and busts.
claims.testable: no: single-stock judgment

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: there's a possibility that there are these big forces that the market is missing
claims.claim: Markets may miss big forces despite efficiency; he turns to psychology to explain why.
claims.testable: partly: requires a measurable big-force variable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: looking backwards. And when you have major changes in things like AI, that muscle that we have, that mental muscle is just not strong enough, right?
claims.claim: Humans imagine the future by looking backward, so big discontinuities such as AI (trillion-dollar firms growing earnings 80-100%) are underestimated by analysts, which is why markets can miss macro forces.
claims.indicator: analyst earnings growth forecasts vs outcomes
claims.testable: yes: compare forecast revisions with realised growth

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: How did Greek bonds before the European financial crisis have lower interest rates than the German bond market, right?
claims.claim: Government bond markets are the most manipulated or paradigm-stuck (Greek yields below Bunds before the euro crisis, Japanese yields staying low as debt rose), and such disconnects can persist; he admits he does not understand them.
claims.indicator: sovereign yield spreads, Japan debt vs yields
claims.testable: partly: spreads and debt data public, persistence hard to forecast

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I think it was in the early 90s European currencies were all linked and then they broke.
claims.claim: Linked or pegged currencies can break suddenly (early 1990s European currencies), and he missed it.
claims.testable: partly: peg breaks are rare events

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: it's really hard to come up with any kind of rule of action. And so we just have to use evidence over cycles
claims.claim: Because the world keeps changing, fixed rules are hard to write, so he relies on evidence across cycles to bias allocation one way or the other.
claims.testable: no: a stance on method

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you just really want to be fully invested in equities as much as you can throughout cycles because it's pretty hard to time again unless the Fed is jamming up um interest rates.
claims.claim: Stay fully invested in equities through cycles because timing is hard, except when the Fed is raising rates sharply.
claims.indicator: Fed rate hikes as exit trigger
claims.testable: yes: backtest buy-and-hold vs hike-conditioned underweight

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we think that real assets can be a little bit of of a better diversifier to your portfolio than just bonds.
claims.claim: The 60/40 premise rests on bond yield and inverse stock-bond correlation; he is biased against it and prefers real assets as a diversifier given current risks.
claims.direction: real assets over bonds as diversifier
claims.conditions: when stock-bond correlation is not negative
claims.testable: yes: test diversifier benefit vs bonds

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So we would be more like 60 70% equities and then 10% maybe real assets and then you know the balance in in bonds.
claims.claim: Illustrative allocation: 60-70% equities, about 10% real assets, remainder bonds; he says there is very little science behind it.
claims.testable: yes: simple fixed-weight portfolio can be backtested

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: So the the optin automatic optin to the markets makes makes a lot of sense.
claims.claim: For people who do not follow markets, an automatic opt-in default with lifetime income makes sense, while those with time and advice can deviate to add value.
claims.testable: no: policy design opinion

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: one is just rebalancing. So when things get out of whack, then we can just uh that we can rebalance our portfolios on a on a quarterly basis or on a price trigger basis.
claims.claim: Rebalancing on a calendar (quarterly) or price-trigger basis is a practical tool for resilience in unpredictable markets.
claims.testable: yes: compare calendar and threshold rebalancing

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: you're just constantly harvesting some of those profits and reinvesting in in oil
claims.claim: In a commodities portfolio, harvesting gold gains last year and reinvesting in oil at $55-60 paid off this year, an example of rebalancing into the laggard.
claims.testable: yes: rebalance rule backtestable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: 10-year interest rates go up 200 basis points and we have a loss of confidence I can tell you nothing's going up even gold doesn't go up
claims.claim: In a Treasury-led confidence shock (10-year yields up 200 bp) even gold falls as holders liquidate whatever they can sell for cash.
claims.conditions: loss of confidence in US government debt
claims.testable: partly: rare episodes, gold-yield relation testable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: people in the in the Middle East were just liquidating. They were selling Treasury bonds and they were selling gold.
claims.claim: In the Iran conflict Middle East holders sold both Treasuries and gold to raise cash, showing safe havens are sold in a cash scramble.
claims.conditions: cash need in a geopolitical shock
claims.testable: partly: single episode

claims.speaker: Alex (host)
claims.quote: it just comes down to having very broad diversification.
claims.claim: Resilience comes from broad diversification across assets that win in different environments, giving up some upside to protect the downside, since the alternative is accurate timing.
claims.testable: yes: compare diversified vs concentrated drawdowns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: if the if the SAS companies in the public markets go down, then they get marked down in the private markets
claims.claim: Private fund software holdings are marked down when public SaaS stocks fall, so private assets add less diversification than their smooth marks suggest.
claims.indicator: public SaaS prices vs private marks
claims.testable: yes: correlation of private marks with public comps

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: then you can't be fooled by the number of line items and different labels that you have.
claims.claim: Judge diversification by underlying risk exposures, not by number of holdings or labels.
claims.testable: yes: exposure decomposition

claims.speaker: Alex (host)
claims.quote: suddenly the the MAG7 are the top holdings in growth funds, value funds, momentum funds, quality funds
claims.claim: The same Magnificent Seven stocks top holdings in growth, value, momentum and quality funds, so style labels hide concentration.
claims.testable: yes: holdings overlap measurable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: Bitcoin's like a teenager has yet to be adopted by a lot of institutional investors
claims.claim: Bitcoin is fundamentally like gold and the other precious metals (platinum, palladium, silver) but at an earlier maturity stage with limited institutional adoption; they do not move in lockstep.
claims.testable: partly: correlation measurable, maturity stage is judgment

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: gold and Bitcoin both hit all-time highs last year and they're both, you know, kind of struggling a little bit this year.
claims.claim: Over a broader view gold and Bitcoin perform similarly: both made highs last year and both struggle this year.
claims.testable: yes: rolling correlation of gold and Bitcoin

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we predicted it would fall this year because of the happening cycle, which is obviously something you don't have in gold
claims.claim: Bitcoin's halving cycle (mining reward halves every four years) was the reason they predicted a fall this year, a cycle absent in gold.
claims.testable: yes: few cycles but dates are known

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I think Bitcoin will survive though, unlike probably a lot of other crypto assets.
claims.claim: Bitcoin will survive while most other crypto assets will not.
claims.testable: no: long-run survival view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I'm really starting to think of them less as one coherent group in a portfolio and and more just you know part of international equity exposure
claims.claim: Emerging markets are too different politically and economically to treat as one bloc, and are better viewed as part of international equity exposure.
claims.testable: partly: country dispersion measurable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: there will be some sort of centrifugal force around them because companies will be able to grow to a bigger scale inside these big consumer markets.
claims.claim: The US, Europe, China and India are four big consumer markets, so firms can scale within each and growth will be pulled to them.
claims.direction: long firms in the four large consumer markets
claims.testable: no: broad structural thesis

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: You can actually diversify globally maybe more so than you have been in for some time.
claims.claim: Countries differ in policy, demographics and technology exposure, so international diversification is attractive now and may not cost return, with possibly higher returns outside the US.
claims.testable: partly: diversification and relative return testable

claims.speaker: Alex (host)
claims.quote: The rupee is just not dollarized in any way. their economic cycle is pretty different from ours.
claims.claim: India offers diversification because the rupee is not dollar-linked and its economic cycle differs from the US.
claims.testable: yes: cycle correlation with the US

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: but then sometimes like within a trend, it can give you some kind of guidance one way or the other at extremes
claims.claim: He does not use valuation at the market or industry level, but within a trend valuation guides at extremes, and he says there is no great answer to the value-versus-trend tension.
claims.conditions: extreme valuation inside an ongoing trend
claims.testable: yes: test valuation-extreme filter on trend signals

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: if a company has no profits, you have to use price to sales.
claims.claim: For unprofitable firms use price-to-sales; Nvidia at 30 to 50 times sales and SpaceX at 100 times sales are extremes he considers worrying.
claims.testable: yes: P/S extreme vs forward returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: there's no valuation support for that stock, right?
claims.claim: Stocks such as SpaceX and Tesla ride a narrative with no valuation support; the company may still be fantastic but investors should know the support is absent.
claims.testable: no: judgment on individual names

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: A lot of times people talk about markets and they take only the valuation as a metric and that just I find is usually doesn't work
claims.claim: Valuation alone fails as a market signal (international markets are cheap yet need another driver), so valuation is less, not un-, important after the trend is framed.
claims.testable: yes: valuation-only vs valuation plus trend

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: this company have an ability you know, to to have with the customer relationships to generate profits three years into a trend
claims.claim: For second-order beneficiaries of themes like AI, ask whether the company has a moat that keeps profits flowing three years into the trend.
claims.testable: partly: moat proxied by margins or returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: Nuclear is more influenced by public policy. There's been a bipartisan shift.
claims.claim: Nuclear demand is policy-driven and policy turned bipartisan and global in favour of nuclear, supporting multi-year demand from power needs.
claims.testable: no: policy view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the inability to turn you know get a mine going in the short term should lead to good you know visible profitability several years out
claims.claim: Copper and other metals demand with supply constraints (mines cannot start quickly) should give visible profitability several years out.
claims.testable: partly: supply lead times measurable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: When's the party getting out of control, right? When have people have one too many drinks, everyone's shouting at each other. When's the time to leave?
claims.claim: Experience gives a gut sense of when sentiment is excessive (the party analogy); he uses it to know when to leave a narrative.
claims.testable: no: gut feel

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: they're not showing price to earnings ratios are price to sales that right there is kind of a signal like they're not profitable
claims.claim: When a hot theme (drone stocks) is quoted on price-to-sales instead of P/E, that is a warning that the companies are unprofitable.
claims.testable: yes: share of unprofitable firms in a theme

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the solutions just don't size it too much like you know dip your toe in the water but don't fall in love with uh you know with that theme
claims.claim: Size narrative positions small, dip a toe and keep an eye on valuation.
claims.testable: partly: sizing rules testable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: last summer they were trading at 40 times forward earnings
claims.claim: Listed alternative asset managers went from a 10x forward P/E IPO discount to market multiples to 40x last summer and back to 10x (Blue Owl), a valuation round trip.
claims.indicator: forward P/E of alternative asset managers
claims.testable: yes: forward P/E vs subsequent returns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: blue alals below its IPO price you know you kind of it gives you a little bit level of comfort and guidance
claims.claim: Valuation works in reverse too: a stock back to a 10x forward P/E below its IPO price, with fundamentals supporting it, gives some comfort that there is value.
claims.indicator: forward P/E, price vs IPO price
claims.testable: yes: IPO price and forward P/E testable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: Van has stayed away from like leveraged ETFs and inverse ETFs
claims.claim: Avoid products whose behaviour differs from the name (leveraged, inverse, dislocated or expensive ETFs) so clients are not surprised.
claims.testable: no: product policy

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: there's no magic bullet just because you're in an index it means your stock can't go down a tremendous amount.
claims.claim: Passive flows do not protect stocks; index membership does not prevent large drops, so focus on index rules and ETF construction rather than fearing indexation.
claims.testable: partly: index membership vs drawdowns

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: we just experienced in the second quarter of 2026 one of the highest dispersion quarters meaning stocks were all over the place
claims.claim: Q2 2026 was one of the highest stock-dispersion quarters, evidence that passive indexing has not made the market uninformative.
claims.testable: yes: dispersion index

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: That ecosystem like if you look at Oracle, that was down 50% in in a in a quarter.
claims.claim: In Q4 last year OpenAI spent heavily with little visible revenue and Oracle fell 50% in a quarter, showing the AI ecosystem can sell off hard.
claims.testable: partly: one episode

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: fixed income markets are the first markets to become less liquid
claims.claim: Fixed income is the first market to lose liquidity in stress, so ETFs that add liquidity help bond investors.
claims.testable: yes: ETF vs bond liquidity in stress

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: certainly group behavior sort of like you saw with meme stocks
claims.claim: Crypto bad behaviour and meme-stock group behaviour make an unhealthy, unlevel market, unlike sober individuals picking stocks.
claims.testable: partly: meme episodes identifiable

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: India, it's not big enough in international equity indices
claims.claim: India is underappreciated and underweight in international equity indices.
claims.testable: partly: index weight vs fundamentals

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: I think that'll bring a little bit of a clearer market structure to India
claims.claim: The expected spin-out of Jio from Reliance would clarify India's tech pillars and give a clearer market structure.
claims.testable: no: corporate event

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: the outsource services companies like Infosys and what have you will have done their wash out correction because of AI
claims.claim: Indian IT outsourcing firms will complete an AI-driven washout correction, leaving the market in a better spot.
claims.testable: no: single-sector view

claims.speaker: Jan van Eck
claims.quote: India suffered a lot because of the Iran war and the US tariffs. So, in a way, I think it's especially good time
claims.claim: India has been hurt by the Iran war and US tariffs, which makes this an especially good time to look at the market after the shock.
claims.testable: no: single view
